ExportControlNote: Emerson's India engineering centres put US export jurisdiction over Indian-developed automation IP.
GE Vernova T&D India is NSE-listed at 51% promoter holding — US export rules reach it regardless.
Indian machine tool builders are FANUC's customers, not competitors — every Indian CNC machine ships a Japanese brain.
Siemens Ltd demerged its India energy business in 2025; capital allocation stays in Munich.
STL is a genuine global peer in fibre — the rare case where an Indian firm out-margins the incumbent.
BASF closing Dahej sulfation units is the clearest evidence Indian mid-caps priced a German multinational out.
Bayer CropScience India pays out ~99% of profit as dividend — a repatriation vehicle, not a growth arm.
NVIDIA allocation under US export rules governs both Dell's backlog and Netweb's growth.
The sharpest illustration of where India's electronics push stands: assembly yes, active photonics zero.
Every Indian fab built increases ASML's revenue and India's equipment import bill simultaneously.
Bosch's Mobility EBIT fell to 1.8% while UNO Minda grew profit 46% — the EV transition is inverting the moat.
Bose licensed its badge to Noise rather than compete — an admission it can't win Indian volume alone.
Indian DC operators build the facility and import the critical infrastructure — same pattern as the fabs.
Continental is exiting everything except tyres — the one business where Indian firms are strongest.
POSCO returned to India as JSW's 50:50 partner after its solo Odisha plan collapsed in 2017.
Sharp is now a brand seeking manufacturing partners; Amber will likely build its Indian ACs.
India is the world's pharmacy and buys nearly every instrument used to make and test the medicine.
India is being brought in as a labour and fabrication base, not a technology partner.
India's whole AC industry runs on Chinese compressors — PLI localises the box, not the value.
Tesla opened a Mumbai showroom, declined to manufacture, and sold 285 EVs in a month.
ITAR governs what India can buy, modify and re-export; offset contracts transfer work, not IP.
Japan is retreating from shipbuilding; the question is whether India takes share as it does.
Indian IP, foreign silicon, US-controlled EDA tools — three layers of dependency in one chip.
India assembles the phone and imports every part that determines its cost.
India's EXIM trade moves on foreign-flagged ships; war-risk and rerouting decisions are made abroad.
Blue Star publicly declined a foreign partnership for DC chillers — the first such refusal in this review.
Namo Bharat: Indian track, French trains, Finnish radio, German operator. Layered dependency.
62% French-state-owned. The AUKUS cancellation showed such contracts can evaporate on geopolitics.
Motherson is the only case here where technology transfer produced a partner larger than the source.
L&T's Electrical & Automation business was sold to Schneider — a Tier A firm that became Tier B.
LG India's IPO prospectus states it: parent-dependent for technology, 1.8–1.9% of sales as royalty, ₹4,700 Cr of tax disputes.
Nikon wrote off ¥90.6B on metal AM — the one segment where India is at a comparable stage.
Foundation-owned and unacquirable. The SMT layer has never been licensed to anyone.
Infineon will have 4,500 Bengaluru engineers by 2030 designing power semiconductors — for Infineon.
75% of Danaher's revenue is recurring consumables — the lock-in Truenat was built to break.
PerkinElmer bought Tulip Diagnostics in 2017. Tulip's founder left and built Molbio — which then displaced Cepheid.
NPPA price capping created the space Indian stent makers took — regulatory sovereignty working in India's favour.
US FDA inspects Indian plants and issues import alerts — a foreign regulator with operational control.
AMD kept ZT Systems' design and sold the factories to Sanmina — the industry telling you where value sits.
The widest gap in this review — wider than EUV or jet engines. India buys the product at whatever price three firms set.
Pixxel paid SpaceX to launch Indian satellites because ISRO had no process for Indian customers.
Honeywell Automation India grew 9% over five years while ABB India and Hitachi Energy grew 25–40%.
Indian firms took $500M+/quarter out of a live Amgen blockbuster in Amgen's home market.
Zydus is attacking a product still growing 12% a quarter — more ambitious than any prior Indian device entry.
DePuy Synthes is being sold for $20B+ — repricing the segment where Indian firms are strongest.
Sandoz's spin-off means Novartis no longer recaptures its own generic erosion — every rupee India takes is lost.
Nayara Energy — Indian-listed, Rosneft-linked — was hit by EU sanctions. The scenario your criteria exist for.
Across FANUC, ABB, Siemens, Infineon and Mitsubishi Electric: India competes at system level, absent at component level.
US law let American firms export reactors to India but barred design or manufacture there — which is why BSMR is indigenous.
Airbus sources $1.6B/yr from India, tripled since 2019 — manufacturing execution, not design authority.
Five foreign firms hold 45–50% of India's industrial automation market — a compounding disadvantage.
China used volume-based procurement to cut FMC's prices. India has NPPA and hasn't used it here.
Two patents in twenty years. This gap exists because nobody bothered, not because it's hard.
MHI's Mogami export is Japan's first modern warship sale. India designs its own frigates and has never exported one.
ELGi's stated weakness is premium technology — narrower than most gaps here, but the same boundary.
Widia reads as Indian — Bangalore HQ, NSE-listed — and is Kennametal-owned. Tungsten is the live Chinese chokepoint.
Netmagic was Indian-built and NTT-owned since 2012. India's sovereign AI compute partly runs on it.
Anchor is 63 years old, Mumbai-founded, Make-in-India branded — and wholly Panasonic-owned since 2007.
Press Note 3 blocked BYD's $1B plant. It sold 285 EVs in a month. The most effective policy instrument in this review.
Sony is going fab-lite via a TSMC joint venture. The July 2026 Kumamoto earthquake suspended sensor production — excluded from guidance, and Indian phone assembly depends on that supply.
'Full IP transfer' is a competitive promise. Kaveri ran 642% over cost and 13 years late with similar commitment.

Pure royalty outflow. Every Indian-assembled phone, TV and now Maruti Suzuki vehicle pays a per-unit fee into pools India has no stake in. The dependency is legal, not physical — there is no factory to build.
HPE localised PCBA with VVDN to claim trusted-supplier status for Indian government procurement, subsidised by PLI — while design authority, firmware and silicon all stay abroad.
Acer runs a 1.9% operating margin — Dixon earns more manufacturing than Acer earns branding. The 5% import-reduction mandate localises assembly, not components.

Rheinmetall came to India for raw materials and supply-chain security — Reliance supplies energetics to German specification. Indian firms also carry live secondary-sanctions risk over where their shells end up.

India's biggest small-arms orders go to Israeli and Russian licensed designs while the indigenous M72 sells to Armenia, Nepal and a British competition. A procurement preference, not a technology gap.

India's largest e-commerce platform (Flipkart), largest fashion platform (Myntra) and largest UPI app (PhonePe) are all Walmart-owned. The Amazon-vs-Flipkart contest shaping Indian policy is between two American companies.
~67% EBITDA margin from licensing membrane containment to every LNG yard on earth, including Korea's and China's. A few hundred people holding a global toll booth.

With Sunic System, the only maker of production-scale OLED deposition equipment at Gen6 and above — supplying essentially all iPhone OLED lines. The reason a funded Indian display fab still could not be built.

The compressor chokepoint appears under Daikin, Trane, LG, Sharp and Panasonic — five entries in the ledger, one underlying dependency. Blue Star can build a data centre chiller and not the compressor inside it.
Every Indian fab under construction will import its vacuum pumps. HHV is Indian-owned with real vacuum engineering and no announced semiconductor programme.
Indian tool makers grind imported carbide on imported machines running imported CNC controllers. Three layers of dependency in one consumable.
The sensor layer beneath every automation entry in the ledger. India competes at the commodity end and is absent in safety-rated and LiDAR classes.
Quietly inside data centres, HVAC and every wind tunnel. India makes the fan and imports the integrated motor-drive-controller unit that gives it efficiency.

The closest thing in the world to a direct analogue of an Indian company — and India has one. Forbes Marshall is family-owned, Pune-based and generational. The gap is Coriolis and analysers, not the model.
India builds laser machines around imported sources. Trumpf also supplies the amplifier for ASML's EUV light source — a second chokepoint sitting behind the first.
Janatics of Coimbatore is genuinely India's Festo — Indian-owned, exporting, with a full pneumatics range. The gap is servo-pneumatics.
The rare-earth magnet chokepoint that appears under Tesla, BYD and Bosch. Chinese export controls on magnets directly threaten Indian EV motor production.
India is the world's second-largest steel producer and imports its rolling mills, casters and mill automation.
The two firms standing between India's PCB push and actually making advanced boards. Amber's Korea Circuit JV and Kaynes Circuits both import this layer.
Not Mittelstand — a four-firm oligopoly — but structurally identical, and the chokepoint under every litre of Indian lubricant including IOCL Servo.
Mitsui & Co did ~¥14tn revenue and ¥834bn profit with ~50,000 consolidated employees, liquidating $9.9bn of assets to fund $16.1bn of capex. Berkshire now holds above 10% of all five sogo shosha.
Marubeni, Canon, Nissan, Yamaha, Resonac, Kubota and JFE. The group where India competes best — and where an Indian champion was quietly acquired.

Itochu leads the five sogo shosha on net profit with ROE of 14.6% against Mitsubishi's 8.5%, earning a narrow moat from non-resource businesses. Kawasaki Heavy, Fujitsu, Furukawa and Isuzu sit alongside it.
Kobe Steel, Sojitz, Ube and Toyo Tire. The group where Indian firms hold the most ground — welding, tyres, cement and aluminium are all genuinely competitive.

The most consequential structure in the comparison. Denso alone did ¥7.16tn revenue and ¥519bn operating profit as the world's second-largest auto supplier. Toyota Industries' 2026 buyout is unwinding the cross-shareholdings for a ¥4.43tn book gain.
A vertical keiretsu spanning grid, rail, machinery, medical and IT. Its Indian grid arm is NSE-listed and Japanese-controlled — one of the clearest Tier B cases in the ledger.

The most India-embedded of the group. AM/NS India's domestic shipments rose year on year in April-June 2026 with EBITDA up 31% quarter on quarter, against Indian steel demand expected at 171.6 million tonnes.

Privately held, ~14,000 employees, roughly £2bn of R&D since 2021 — about £9m a week. FY24 revenue £6.6bn with pre-tax profit down 49% to £561m despite record 20m+ units; FY25 grew EBITDA 18% on 13 launches. HQ returning from Singapore to the UK in 2026.

Record FY25 revenue $7.054bn (+15%), backlog $11.4bn, and the $34.9bn Ansys acquisition closed July 2025. Design IP fell 21% in Q4 on US export restrictions in China — the formal ban lasted six weeks but the revenue damage persisted for quarters. India's own DLI and Chips-to-Startup programmes are delivered through these tools.

FY25 revenue $5.297bn (+14%) at a 44.6% non-GAAP operating margin — smaller than Synopsys but far more profitable. IP revenue grew ~25% while Synopsys's fell 21% in the same China-restricted year. Backlog $7.8bn; 2026 guidance explicitly assumes export controls remain substantially similar.

FY25 revenue $29.8bn (+3.2%) at an 8.9% gross margin and 6.3% core operating margin — bigger than Sanmina, less profitable per dollar. Intelligent Infrastructure grew 34% while Connected Living fell 25%. India footprint doubled in a year: 500,000 to 1.2 million sq ft, headcount 5,000 to almost 11,000, with a new Pune plant opened June 2026 and a ₹2,000 crore Tamil Nadu MoU. Five customers are ~38% of revenue.

Group sales €20,495m, down 5.1% nominally — FX took 4.2%, divestments 1.7%, leaving organic growth of just +0.9%, price-driven with volume flat. Adhesive Technologies grew 1.5% organically at a 16.5-17.5% return on sales; €525m of cost savings realised. In India the roles reverse: Pidilite holds ~70% of the organised consumer adhesive market at a 22.5% EBITDA margin, above Henkel's own 14.5-15.5% group margin.

Korea's largest chaebol by every measure. Samsung Electronics alone did $220.7bn in 2025 and holds the number one position globally in semiconductors, having overtaken Intel in 2024. The group spans ~60 affiliates — Life Insurance, C&T, SDI, Heavy Industries, SDS and Biologics. Beyond Electronics, already covered separately in this ledger, the group's reach into biologics, batteries and construction is where India's comparison actually sits.

Hyundai Motor did ₩175.23tn revenue with ₩14.24tn operating income on 4.15 million vehicles and 126,407 employees. The group targets 12% global EV share by 2030 and spans Kia, Genesis, Mobis, Hyundai Steel, Glovis, Rotem and Boston Dynamics. Hyundai Motor India's 2024 IPO followed the same OFS pattern as LG's — proceeds to the Korean parent.

Korea's second-largest chaebol, spanning SK hynix (covered separately), SK Innovation, SK Telecom, SK On, SK Siltron and SK ie technology. The group is the clearest illustration of vertical integration in memory — wafers, cells, separators and chips inside one family-controlled structure.

LG and GS were one company until the Koo and Huh families split in 2005; LG took electronics and chemicals. Beyond LG Electronics, covered separately, the group spans LG Chem, LG Energy Solution, LG Display and LG Innotek — which is where the India comparison actually bites.

The most defence-focused of the major chaebols. Hanwha Aerospace has become significant in global defence exports, particularly artillery systems — which places it in direct competition with India's ATAGS programme for the same export customers. The group also spans Hanwha Ocean (shipbuilding), Hanwha Systems and Hanwha Qcells (solar).

The smallest of the groups here and the most directly comparable to Indian PSUs. Doosan Enerbility is one of a handful of firms globally that can forge and machine a nuclear reactor pressure vessel — a business L&T Hazira is already in.

The consumer-and-commodity tier of the chaebol system — Lotte in chemicals, food and retail, GS in energy, retail and construction after splitting from LG in 2005. This is the group where India competes most completely.

The most complete corporate reinvention in the ledger — a film company that now earns from semiconductor materials, biologics and medical devices. Revenue ¥3.357tn (+5.0%), record on all three profit lines. Semiconductor Materials grew 31.3% in a single quarter on AI demand, while Bio CDMO profitability slipped enough to force a guidance cut from ¥69bn to ¥41bn. Silver prices cut Healthcare operating income 34.7% in Q4.

Net sales ¥4.6tn (+2.5%), top-ten in US patents for 42 consecutive years. Industrial is only 8% of revenue and is the reason this entry matters: Canon says its back-end lithography sets the industry standard for leading-edge semiconductor packaging — the exact layer India is building. Canon also owns Canon Tokki, the OLED evaporator duopolist already logged separately here.

FY2025 revenue NT$3,809.05bn (~$122.42bn, +35.9%), net income NT$1,717.88bn, Q4 gross margin 62.3% and operating margin 54.0%. Holds ~69.9% of the global foundry market against Samsung's 7.2%. Deployed 305 process technologies and made 12,682 products for 534 customers on over 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers. 2026 capex guided at $52-56bn. Advanced nodes at 7nm and below are 74-77% of wafer revenue; HPC is 58% and rising past 61%. North America is 75% of net revenue.

2025 revenue NT$8.1tn (~$260bn, +18%), operating profit NT$259.2bn (+29%), net profit NT$189.4bn (+24%) — records on every line. Gross margin 6.15%, operating margin 3.20%, net margin 2.34%. Over 40% of the global EMS market, 240+ campuses in 24 countries and around 900,000 employees at peak. India's largest private electronics employer, and the company through which most of India's smartphone export numbers actually flow.

Post-Solventum separation in April 2024, 3M runs three segments — Safety & Industrial, Transportation & Electronics, and Consumer — on roughly $24-25bn of revenue. Its distinguishing asset is around 60 technology platforms recombined across tens of thousands of products, and it faces three separate Indian champions already in this ledger: CUMI on abrasives, Pidilite on adhesives and Healthium on medical consumables.

The world's largest medical device company at roughly $33.5bn, though J&J MedTech at ~$31.9bn is closing and the planned MiniMed diabetes separation ($2.8bn of revenue) may cost Medtronic the top spot. Q3 FY26 revenue $9.0bn (+8.7% reported, +6.0% organic) was the strongest growth in ten quarters, driven by Cardiac Ablation Solutions up 80% — 137% in the US — on pulsed field ablation. This company holds most of the device gaps already logged under Abbott and Boston Scientific.

The blind spot this ledger carried until now. India is the world's second-largest textile producer and among the largest employers in the sector, and it imports the great majority of its spinning, weaving, texturising and processing machinery. Rieter is Swiss and listed, Trützschler is German and family-owned, Oerlikon holds Barmag and Neumag, and Picanol is Belgian. Lakshmi Machine Works of Coimbatore is the only Indian maker at scale.

Included as the empirical test case rather than as a competitor. Entity-listed by the US in May 2019, Huawei lost simultaneous access to EDA tools, TSMC foundry capacity and Google's Android licence — the exact three dependencies this ledger flags for India. Its response, the HiSilicon Kirin 9000S on SMIC process and HarmonyOS, is the only real-world evidence of what a large economy can rebuild under full technology denial, and at what cost. FY2024 revenue was CNY 862.1bn; later figures should be verified directly.

FY2026 revenue $215.9bn, up 65%, with Q4 alone at $68.1bn and Data Center at $62.3bn (+75%). Full-year net income $120bn at a 71.3% non-GAAP gross margin. The April 2025 H20 licence requirement for China cost a $4.5bn charge and demonstrated that a single US licensing decision can remove a market overnight — the same instrument that would govern any Indian AI build-out.

The largest semiconductor equipment company by revenue, running roughly $27bn across Semiconductor Systems, Applied Global Services and Display. Where ASML holds patterning, Applied holds nearly everything else — deposition, etch, ion implantation, CMP and metrology. Every fab India builds will buy the majority of its tool set from Applied, Lam and Tokyo Electron.

On 21 February 2025 Western Digital completed the separation of its Flash business into an independent Sandisk Corporation, leaving WD as a pure-play hard disk drive company. That leaves HDD as a three-supplier industry — Seagate, WD and Toshiba — supplying the nearline storage under every hyperscale data centre. The Board raised the quarterly dividend 25% to $0.125 on FY26 momentum. This entire category was absent from the ledger until now.

Separated from Western Digital on 21 February 2025 as an independent NAND flash company, having been wholly owned before that. It joins Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron and YMTC in an industry where India has no presence at any layer — and where the memory price shock already logged under SK hynix and Dell hits Indian assemblers directly. India's one entrant here is MiPhi Semiconductors, the Micromax–Phison joint venture designing NAND storage silicon in Bengaluru.

FY2025 revenue NT$595,966m (+12.3%) with 2025 gross profit NT$283,080m and Q4 revenue NT$150,188m on the Dimensity 9500 ramp. Around 22,500 employees and roughly 1.5 billion devices a year. The company whose silicon sits inside the majority of India's smartphones — and which runs large design centres in Bengaluru and Noida employing Indian engineers to design chips India does not own.

The world's largest outsourced assembly and test provider, and the direct competitor to everything India's OSAT programme is building. Where TSMC holds CoWoS in-house, ASE holds the merchant advanced packaging market that Indian OSATs will have to win business against.

The Taiwanese ODM tier that designs and builds most of the world's notebooks and a large share of AI servers. Quanta alone did roughly $35bn with 56,700 employees. This group contains the ledger's clearest reverse-acquisition story: Wistron sold its Indian iPhone plant to Tata Electronics in 2023, converting a Taiwanese ODM site into Indian ownership.

FY2025 revenue $17.9bn with $2.7bn operating income and $2.0bn net income across 83,000 employees and roughly 200 facilities. Known for DC fans, data centre rectifiers and switching power supplies — the components inside almost every system in this ledger. Delta has substantial Indian manufacturing, which makes it a Tier B presence competing directly with Indian power electronics firms.

Company: Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB & Zhen Ding
ExportControlNote: The substrate layer India's entire electronics policy sits on top of and does not address. IC substrates — the mini-PCB that carries a chip inside its package — are held by Ibiden and Shinko in Japan and Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB and Zhen Ding in Taiwan. Every Indian OSAT will import them, and no Indian producer exists at any level.

Two Swedish firms holding both ends of the hard-materials business — mining and rock excavation equipment, and the carbide cutting tools that appear in the Silmax entry. Epiroc was spun out of Atlas Copco in 2018. India is the world's second-largest coal producer and imports most of its underground mining equipment.

Three Swedish firms holding component positions inside almost every machine in this ledger — SKF on bearings, Alfa Laval on heat exchangers and separators, Trelleborg on engineered polymers. India competes credibly on bearings and heat transfer and not at all on high-speed and specialty classes.

The world's largest wind turbine maker by installed capacity, and one of the few foreign incumbents in this ledger facing genuine Indian competition at system level. Suzlon designs and manufactures its own turbines; India's constraint is offshore and the largest onshore platforms, not onshore wind itself.

The company whose GLP-1 franchise defines the largest therapeutic opportunity in global pharma, and the one where India's position changed materially: the Indian patent on semaglutide expired in March 2026, opening the market to Indian generics years before Western markets. India has 89.8 million diabetics and the world's largest generic industry.

The Nordic marine and defence cluster. Wärtsilä holds large marine engines — already logged as a chokepoint under HD Hyundai and Imabari. Kongsberg holds maritime systems and missiles. Saab is the one with real Indian manufacturing: Carl-Gustaf M4 production in Haryana, its first such plant outside Sweden.

FY2025 comparable sales up 2% with order intake up 6%, and adjusted EBITA margin up 80 basis points to 12.3% despite tariffs. The segments diverged sharply: Personal Health grew 8% at an 18.0% margin, Connected Care 3% at 10.7%, and Diagnosis & Treatment was flat at 11.7%. Free cash flow absorbed a €1,025 million payment for the Respironics recall settlements in the US. It launched the Azurion neuro biplane platform and showed 3.0T helium-free MR — which matters for India, because VoxelGrids reached a near-helium-free 1.5T scanner from the other direction.

A hard year: FY2025 revenue fell 11.1% to $11.80bn, gross margin compressed from 39.3% to 33.9%, and operating income collapsed from $1.68bn to $175 million on $376 million of impairment and restructuring from a global manufacturing reshaping programme. Automotive was down 24% and Power & Discrete down 31.5%. Q4 marked a return to year-over-year growth. It still generated $2,573 million of operating cash flow and is pivoting capital into 300mm silicon, 200mm SiC, advanced packaging and the NXP MEMS acquisition. ST's Greater Noida campus is its largest design centre outside Europe — India engineers this silicon and owns none of it.

Not a company but an ownership class, and it belongs in this ledger for the same reason Maersk does. Greek owners control the largest share of the world merchant fleet by tonnage — dry bulk, tankers and increasingly LNG — through privately held family firms. India's EXIM trade, energy imports and coal imports move substantially on tonnage owned in Athens and Piraeus.

A record $1.28bn global box office in 2025, up 40%, with Asia-Pacific roughly half of that and up nearly 80% year on year. India is a named growth market: IMAX has historically been anchored by PVR INOX and is broadening to Mirage Cinema and Rajhans, with Indian screen count projected past 150 by 2029. The business model is the point — IMAX licenses the format and takes a share of box office. India makes more films than any country, runs a record $1.48bn theatrical market, and owns none of the premium format technology its audiences pay extra for.

The strongest year in the group's history. IDG did $58.9bn (+17%) holding a record 24.4% global PC share — the widest lead over the number two in fifteen years; ISG hit a record $19.2bn (+32%) and turned profitable for the first time; SSG passed $10bn (+19%) at over 20% operating margin. AI-related revenue reached 38% of group revenue in Q4, up 84%. Chinese-owned, and its Motorola smartphones are manufactured in India by Dixon — which is the whole India story in one line.

A whole equipment class the ledger had no entry for, in the country with the largest agricultural workforce on earth — and one of India's strongest showings anywhere. Mahindra is the world's largest tractor manufacturer by volume, with TAFE, Escorts Kubota and Sonalika behind it. The gap is not the tractor. It is the precision guidance layer bolted on top of it, and the processing machinery downstream of the field.

India is the world's second-largest cement producer and this had no entry in the ledger. It is also one of India's clearest ownership reversals: Adani bought Holcim's entire Indian business — Ambuja and ACC — in 2022, taking a European major's India operations into Indian hands. The gap is not the cement; it is the plant that makes it.

The clearest ownership reversal in the ledger. On 10 December 2025 AkzoNobel completed the sale of Akzo Nobel India — including the Dulux brand — to JSW Group at an enterprise value of about €1.4bn on a 25x EBITDA multiple, for up to ₹12,915 crore including the open offer. The entity is now JSW Dulux Ltd. A Dutch major's Indian business moved into Indian hands, alongside Adani buying Holcim's Ambuja and ACC and Tata buying Wistron's iPhone plant. AkzoNobel retained the India powder coatings business and its International Research Centre.

Privately held Danish catalyst house sitting on top of Indian fertiliser and refining. Every Indian urea plant runs ammonia and syngas catalysts from Topsoe, Clariant, Johnson Matthey or KBR. The one place India answers back is refining, where Indian Oil R&D licenses its own INDMAX and IndAdeptG processes.

Norway's nitrogen chemistry major, and the closest thing to a global standard-setter in urea and specialty crop nutrition. India produces urea at enormous scale through IFFCO, RCF and Chambal on imported gas, and Yara Marine's scrubber and shore-power business is where the company touches shipping.

The company that supplies the plant to the world's second-largest cement producer. India makes the cement and imports the kiln line, the mills and the pyroprocessing. FLSmidth also holds minerals processing, where Puzzolana and Propel genuinely compete at the crushing end.

A family-held Swiss firm holding something close to a global position in grain milling, in a country that is the world's largest producer of milk, pulses and several grains and mills them on imported machinery. Bühler also holds die casting machinery for the structural castings EVs and aerospace need.

Swiss pump and rotating equipment maker, and one of the European entries where India competes outright. Kirloskar Brothers is world-class in process pumps, CRI and Shakti hold volume, and Triveni Turbine carries genuine turbomachinery design authority in the service and overhaul business alongside it.

Two businesses in one Swiss firm: piping systems, where Astral, Supreme and Finolex compete fully in India, and GF Machining Solutions in EDM and high-precision machining, where Electronica of Pune is the Indian counterpart and Intech Additive covers metal printing.

Coordinate metrology alongside Zeiss and Mitutoyo, plus a design and simulation software arm holding MSC Nastran and Adams. Precision measurement gates every precision-manufacturing gap in this ledger, and Sipcon and Accurate Gauging operate below that class. Zeus Numerix is India's sole CAE product company.

One of the four global elevator majors, and a rare case of outright Indian category leadership: Johnson Lifts outsells KONE, Otis and Schindler by volume in India. What Indian makers buy in is the traction machine and control system — the value-dense half of the product.

Finnish lifting major. India competes genuinely at industrial crane class through ElectroMech, ACE, Anupam and TIL, and its port expansion runs largely on Chinese ZPMC ship-to-shore cranes rather than Indian or Finnish ones.

Swiss construction chemicals major competing in India against Pidilite, which holds roughly 70% of the organised adhesive market at a margin above Sika's own. Waterproofing, tile adhesives and admixtures are all Indian-led categories.

The third of the global elevator majors present in India, and outsold on volume domestically by Johnson Lifts. The competitive question is the same as for KONE and Otis: Indian makers win on installation and service and buy the drive and control system.

The world's largest pharmaceutical CDMO, and one of the clearest cases of Indian parity. Syngene, Biocon Biologics, Enzene and Laurus are direct peers at materially lower cost, Divi's and Neuland lead in small molecule, and ImmunoACT has an approved CAR-T at a fraction of Western pricing.

The largest flavours and fragrances house in the world. India has genuine aroma chemical manufacture through SH Kelkar, Privi Speciality and Oriental Aromatics, and supplies a large share of global menthol — one of the sectors where Indian chemistry competes on merit rather than cost alone.

Italy's state-anchored defence champion, structurally similar to Thales. India competes credibly across most of its range: BEL and Data Patterns on radar and defence electronics, HAL on rotorcraft with Dhruv, Prachand and LUH, and ISRO with TASL on space systems.

One of the world's largest shipbuilders and a competitor to India's yards in the export market. Mazagon Dock, GRSE and Cochin Shipyard design and build India's own frigates; the submarine design layer and cruise shipbuilding remain outside Indian capability.

One of a handful of firms worldwide that can build a heavy-duty gas turbine. Hot-section metallurgy is the same barrier that defeated the Kaveri engine programme. BHEL assembles smaller frames under licence and Triveni Turbine holds India's only genuine turbomachinery design authority.

The world's largest cable maker, and an industry where India competes fully at conventional voltages. Polycab, KEI and Apar hold power cable; Sterlite Technologies makes its own optical preform. The gap is submarine and interconnector class cable for offshore wind and island links.

The premium braking specialist. India's volume tiers are held outright by Brakes India, Endurance and Rane; carbon-ceramic and motorsport braking has no Indian entrant and is a small, high-margin niche.

Automotive body-shop and powertrain automation, spun out of Stellantis. Indian integrators — Difacto, Systemantics, TAL Manufacturing — handle line integration; the robot arms and the process know-how above them are foreign.

The sharpest single gap in Italian industry for India: IMA and its peers supply the high-speed blister, cartoning and aseptic filling lines that pack a fifth of the world's medicines, made in India. ACG Worldwide is the one Indian firm competing at that class.

Belgian materials group holding cathode active materials, automotive catalysts and precious metal recycling. Epsilon Advanced Materials and Altmin are building cathode capacity, Attero and Lohum lead battery recycling, and Hindustan Platinum holds the precious metal chemistry without the catalyst formulation above it.

The specialty spin-off from Solvay. India holds world-leading positions in several surfactant and fine chemical molecules through Galaxy Surfactants and Fine Organics, and imports the aerospace and electronics-grade polymers that Syensqo, DuPont and Toray hold.

The world's largest steel wire transformation company, and a direct Indian competitor exists: Rajratan Global Wire of Indore is among the largest bead wire producers globally, with Usha Martin and Tata Steel Wires alongside it. A narrow niche where an Indian firm reached world scale.

Airport baggage handling and warehouse automation. India competes genuinely in warehouse and parcel sortation through Addverb, GreyOrange and Falcon Autotech, and every major Indian airport terminal runs an imported baggage system.

Dredger builder to the world. India's port programme and Sagarmala depend on dredging capacity, and the Dredging Corporation of India operates an imported fleet. Cochin Shipyard builds hulls and imports the dredging plant that goes on them.

Dutch family-held shipbuilder built on standardised vessel platforms sold worldwide. India builds tugs, OPVs and support vessels credibly through Cochin Shipyard, Goa Shipyard and Titagarh; the standardised-platform export model is what Indian yards have not replicated.

The world's largest water and waste services group, and an area where India genuinely competes: VA Tech Wabag designs, builds and operates municipal water, wastewater and desalination plants internationally, with Ion Exchange and Thermax on industrial water and Re Sustainability on waste.

Water treatment technology and the consumables inside it. Ion Exchange India makes its own resins — a rare Indian position in process chemistry — while RO and filtration membranes remain held by DuPont, Toray and LG Chem with no Indian producer at scale.

Water infrastructure equipment. India competes fully on pumps through Kirloskar Brothers, CRI and Shakti, and on smart water metering through Genus Power and Secure Meters as national AMI programmes roll out.

Half of the airliner duopoly and among India's largest defence suppliers by value. India has never built a commercial aircraft and has no programme; it does build fuselage sections and structures for Boeing on merit through Tata Advanced Systems, Dynamatic and Aequs.

The hardest gap in the ledger. GE holds the engine position that GTRE's Kaveri failed against over forty years and that the Safran-GTRE AMCA partnership is now trying to route around, fifty years after Snecma took the same path through CFM. Azad Engineering and MTAR already supply GE with hot-section airfoils — India makes the hardest parts of an engine it cannot build.

The world's largest in-vitro diagnostics company and a major oncology franchise. India supplies reagents and lower-tier analysers through Transasia and Agappe, and holds one genuine world-class product in Molbio's Truenat molecular platform, which is WHO-endorsed and deployed globally.

Patented oncology and immunology, where global pharma margin concentrates and Indian firms enter only after expiry. India is a global force in biosimilars through Biocon, Dr Reddy's and Intas, and supplies a fifth of the world's generics, while running almost no novel discovery of its own.

Half of the GLP-1 duopoly with Novo Nordisk. The Indian semaglutide patent expired in March 2026, putting Sun, Cipla, Dr Reddy's, Biocon and Zydus into obesity generics years ahead of Western markets — with the injection device, not the molecule, as the remaining barrier.

India assembles a large and rising share of the world's iPhones through Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron, and Tata bought Wistron's Indian plant outright in 2023. What India does not hold is the silicon, the operating system or the app-store economics — the distinction the whole ledger turns on.

Application processors, modems and RF front ends, plus a licensing arm that is the template for the standard-essential patent chokepoint. India assembles the world's phones and designs none of the silicon inside them; Signalchip and Aheesa are early and sub-scale.

Record €40bn in 2025 at 9% organic growth, €7.5bn adjusted EBITA and record €4.6bn free cash flow, led by data centre demand. It is also the most consequential acquirer of Indian capability in this ledger: it bought L&T's Electrical & Automation business, converting a Tier A champion into a foreign division.

Wiring devices and UPS, where Havells competes outright on switches and Goldmedal and Elmex hold volume tiers. Legrand bought Numeric, once an independent Indian UPS champion, which is why that category now reads foreign-controlled.

With SIG, effectively a duopoly in aseptic carton filling. India is the world's largest milk producer and every dairy carton line is imported. Nichrome and Rajkumar Agro operate at mid-speed and nothing approaches aseptic class.

Global packaging converter, and a category where India genuinely leads: Uflex is among the world's largest flexible packaging makers and EPL is the world's largest laminated tube manufacturer. Barrier and recyclable structures are competitive too.

The largest beverage can maker in the world. India's canned beverage volume is growing quickly and can body manufacture is largely foreign-plant or imported, with Hindustan Tin Works and AGI Greenpac covering adjacent metal and glass containers.

China's display majors, which together dominate global LCD and are taking OLED share from Samsung Display. India assembles modules and fabricates no panels — the largest single unaddressed gap in Indian electronics, unattempted since Vedanta-Innolux was shelved.

China's foundry, built and expanded under full US export control, and the most instructive counterfactual in the ledger. SMIC reached 7nm without EUV at poor yield and high cost. India's Dholera fab targets the same mature-node class on licensed PSMC process technology, with no comparable forcing function and no domestic process development.

The Dutch firm behind ASML that nobody names. ASM holds atomic layer deposition, which every advanced node depends on, alongside epitaxy and thermal deposition. HHV in Bengaluru builds thin-film and vacuum systems at defence grade and has never been funded to reach fab grade.

Die attach, flip chip and hybrid bonding — the equipment class India's OSATs will buy first, and the enabling tool for 3D stacked packaging and HBM. Kaynes Semicon and Avalon hold precision assembly capability and build none of the tools.

Segment: Power tools, hand tools & engineered fastening
ExportControlNote: Founded 1843, roughly 43,500 employees. Tools & Outdoor did $13.2bn in 2025, 87% of company revenue, with sales down 2% and organic down 4% on weak retail power tool demand — but segment margin up 400 basis points to 13.2% on pricing, tariff mitigation and supply chain cuts. Full-year gross margin 30.3%. Engineered Fastening grew 6% on automotive and aerospace, and the company agreed to divest its Consolidated Aerospace Manufacturing business for $1.8bn in cash. India competes strongly on hand tools and fasteners and holds almost nothing in cordless power tools.

Founded 1985 in Hong Kong with around 30,000 employees, and the reason the power tool aisle is less competitive than it looks: Milwaukee, Ryobi in most Western markets, AEG, Hart, Empire and Stiletto sit under one owner, alongside a licence to build Ridgid power tools for Home Depot and the Hoover, Vax and Dirt Devil floorcare brands. India buys the output and holds none of the platform.

Founded 1915 and the last major independent in power tools — no umbrella group above it, roughly ten manufacturing plants and sales in over forty countries. That independence is the point for this ledger: Makita shows a single-brand tool company can hold global scale, which is the shape an Indian entrant would have to take rather than the conglomerate route.

Founded 1920, and structurally the opposite of a volume tool maker: it sells premium automotive and industrial tools through a van-based franchise model directly to technicians, and owns Bahco, Williams, Sioux and Norbar Torque among roughly two dozen brands. India competes on the tool and not on the distribution model.

A decentralised American industrial group running dozens of businesses on a common 80/20 operating model, spanning construction fasteners (Buildex, Ramset, Tapcon, Red Head), welding through Miller and Hobart, and Paslode nail guns. India competes credibly in welding and fasteners and imports the anchoring systems.

Spun out of Danaher in 2016 and holding the instruments engineers actually trust — Fluke in electrical test, Tektronix in oscilloscopes, Keithley in precision measurement, plus Matco automotive tools. It sits directly on top of India's electronics and semiconductor ambitions: you cannot design or qualify what you cannot measure.

Family-controlled through the Martin Hilti Family Trust and structurally unlike every other tool company here: it sells direct to the construction site through its own sales force rather than through retail, bundles tools with anchors, design software and fleet management, and takes the whole system rather than the tool. India builds at enormous scale and imports the certified anchors that hold it together.

Founded 1993 in Nanjing and the clearest demonstration of what India has not done. Chervon bought Skil and Skilsaw from Bosch in 2017, built EGO into a leading cordless outdoor brand, owns FLEX and Devon, and manufactures Kobalt cordless tools for Lowe's. A Chinese firm that went from contract manufacturer to brand owner in three decades — the exact path Indian EMS firms are attempting now.

The largest construction and mining equipment maker in the world, and the holder of autonomous haulage through MineStar. India competes at the volume tiers — backhoes, compaction, road building — and imports the large mining classes outright. Coal India, the world's largest coal producer, runs a substantially imported fleet.

Japan's answer to Caterpillar, holding ultra-class mining trucks and the FrontRunner autonomous haulage system. BEML assembles ultra-class trucks under licence with no indigenous design behind them, which is the pattern across India's mining fleet.

Family-held across Germany and Switzerland, and the broadest range in heavy equipment: tower cranes, mobile and crawler cranes, mining excavators, concrete plant and its own hydraulics and gearboxes. Tower cranes matter for India specifically — the country is in a sustained high-rise construction cycle and ACE is the only Indian maker at that class.

Owner of Potain, the reference tower crane brand, with an Indian plant at Pune building for domestic and export markets. India runs one of the world's largest construction programmes and ACE is the only Indian firm making tower cranes at that class — the rest of the market is Potain, Liebherr and increasingly Zoomlion and XCMG.

One of three firms that build and lay the submarine cables carrying essentially all intercontinental internet traffic. India is among the world's largest internet markets with landing stations at Mumbai, Chennai and Cochin, and Tata Communications owns one of the largest subsea networks on earth — but the cable, the repeaters and the ships that lay and repair them are all foreign.

Sold by Nokia to the French state in 2024, which is itself the point: France treated submarine cable manufacture and the ships that lay it as a strategic asset to be nationalised rather than a business to be sold. ASN builds cable, repeaters and the wet plant, and operates its own fleet. India, with comparable internet scale, has neither.

IndianChampion: Adani Ports / Shipping Corporation of India
ExportControlNote: Founded 1970 with one second-hand vessel and now the largest container line in history — the first to operate a 1,000-ship fleet, roughly 7.3 million TEU of capacity and about 21% of global container capacity, some 57% larger than Maersk. Privately held by the Aponte family from Geneva, with no public accounts. Its India position is now structural: MSC bought 49% of Adani's Vizhinjam port for $1.4bn and is the sole commercial partner behind that port's 1.3 million TEU first year.

The dominant supplier of drilling equipment worldwide — the saying in the industry is that no rig gets built without it. India operates rigs through ONGC, Jindal Drilling and Aban Offshore and manufactures essentially none of the equipment on them. L&T fabricates the platform; NOV supplies what sits on top.

The largest oilfield services company in the world, holding wireline logging, reservoir characterisation and drilling services, plus the Petrel and DELFI software that is the industry's interpretation standard. India's oil and gas sector is an operator sector: ONGC and Oil India run the fields and license the technology.
TechnipFMC's surface business — wellheads and pressure control for onshore and shallow-water production, certification-gated and imported into India at every level.

IndianChampion: None — India owns no subsea construction vessel
ExportControlNote: One of the two firms that physically install and maintain everything on the deepwater seabed, running a fleet of purpose-built construction, pipelay and dive-support vessels. This is the gap the ledger kept pointing at from other cards: India operates deepwater fields and owns no vessel of this class, so every installation and every repair in Indian waters is contracted to a foreign fleet.

Norway's subsea engineering house, holding subsea production systems, umbilicals and the front-end engineering behind North Sea and deepwater developments — and increasingly offshore wind foundations and carbon storage. It is the clearest example of a country converting an oil and gas equipment base into an offshore energy transition business, which is the path India's fabricators have not taken.

The third of the big three oilfield firms, and the one with a second life: alongside drilling and completion equipment it holds industrial turbomachinery through the former GE Oil & Gas, supplying LNG compression trains and gas turbines. India is building LNG import and gas infrastructure at scale and buys this equipment entirely.

The second of the big three, strongest in completions, cementing, stimulation and drilling fluids, with Landmark as the alternative to SLB's subsurface software. India's onshore and offshore fields are worked by these firms under contract; ONGC and Oil India own the acreage and buy the technology on it.

The world's largest seamless steel pipe producer at over three million tonnes of annual capacity, dominating oil country tubular goods with integrated mills across the Americas, Europe and Asia and a Rig Direct model that ships pipe from mill to rig. This is the one part of the oil and gas equipment chain where India genuinely competes — Welspun Corp is among the largest steel pipe producers in the world, and Welspun, Jindal SAW and PSL together hold over 70% of Indian installed capacity.

The French premium tubular specialist, and the holder of VAM — the connection benchmark for gas-tight seals in deepwater and offshore drilling. Vallourec is the clearest illustration of where value sits in this chain: India makes pipe at world scale and buys the thread that goes on the end of it.

The fourth of the international oilfield service firms, strongest in managed pressure drilling, tubular running services, artificial lift and well construction. It matters here because it defines the floor: even the smallest of the internationals holds capability India has no domestic equivalent for at any level.

Italy's offshore engineering and construction contractor, running heavy-lift, pipelay and drilling vessels alongside a large onshore EPC business. Saipem is the direct competitor to L&T Hydrocarbon in offshore EPC — and the comparison is instructive, because L&T wins fabrication scope on merit and Saipem holds the vessels that install what L&T builds.

The largest operator of work-class remotely operated vehicles in the world, plus subsea inspection, survey, umbilicals and offshore project services. Every deepwater intervention anywhere depends on a work-class ROV, and India's underwater vehicle capability sits in NIOT and DRDO at research scale with nothing commercial behind it.

Custom silicon for hyperscalers — AI accelerators, DPUs, optical DSPs and storage controllers designed to order for cloud operators who want an alternative to buying NVIDIA. Marvell runs large design centres in India, which is the point: Indian engineers design this silicon and no Indian firm owns any of it.

The only credible alternative to NVIDIA in AI accelerators and to Intel in server CPUs, holding EPYC, Instinct and the Xilinx adaptive computing portfolio. AMD's largest design footprint outside the US is in India — Bengaluru and Hyderabad — which makes it the clearest illustration of the ledger's central point about design labour versus design ownership.

The largest analog semiconductor company in the world, running its own fabs and holding tens of thousands of catalogue parts that sit in nearly every electronic system built. Analog is the most realistic Indian entry point in silicon — it does not need leading-edge nodes, it rewards circuit skill over process, and Vervesemi and C2i already have parts in production.

With Applied Materials and Tokyo Electron, one of three firms holding the etch and deposition steps that shape every transistor. Lam is dominant in etch specifically — and etch is where 3D NAND and gate-all-around structures are actually formed. India's fabs will buy this tool set entirely.

The other half of the x86 duopoly, the owner of Altera's FPGA business, and now a foundry attempting to win external customers. Intel matters to this ledger less for its products than for what it demonstrates: even a company with its own fabs, its own process and forty years of scale has struggled to hold leading-edge manufacturing — which is the barrier India's fab programme is measured against.

One of three DRAM makers and a major NAND producer — and the anchor tenant of India's semiconductor programme. The Sanand assembly and test plant in Gujarat is India's flagship semiconductor investment, and it is an important distinction that it packages and tests memory rather than fabricating it: the wafers arrive from Taiwan, Japan and the US.

Segment: Custom AI silicon, networking & infrastructure software
ExportControlNote: FY2025 revenue $63.9bn, up 24%, split across two mega-cap businesses: Semiconductor Solutions at $36.9bn and Infrastructure Software at $27.0bn, up 26% on VMware Cloud Foundation. AI hardware alone grew 65% to $20bn, Q4 non-GAAP operating margin hit 66.2%, and free cash flow approached $27bn. It holds roughly 70% of the custom AI accelerator design services market on a $73bn hardware backlog, with an OpenAI agreement to co-develop accelerators and Ethernet for 10 gigawatts of compute from the second half of 2026. Two chokepoints under one roof — the switch silicon most cloud fabrics run on, and the custom silicon hyperscalers use to avoid buying NVIDIA.

FY2025 to 1 November: revenue $11.0bn, up 17%, at a 69.3% gross margin and 41.9% operating margin, with $4.3bn of free cash flow — 39% of revenue. Industrial alone was $4.93bn. Those margins are the point: analog is not a volume business, it is a catalogue and precision business, which is exactly why it is the most realistic silicon entry for India. Vervesemi and C2i already ship parts including space-grade. What ADI has that they do not is forty years of catalogue and the guarantee that a part will still be available in fifteen.

FY2026 to 30 June: revenue $13.58bn, GAAP net income $4.83bn, with roughly $3.9bn of free cash flow over the trailing year. The least visible of the equipment majors and among the most decisive: yield learning is what makes a fab economic rather than merely operational, and KLA holds inspection and metrology close to a monopoly. That puts process control on the critical path of every Indian fab regardless of node.

Record FY2026: net sales ¥2,443.5bn to 31 March 2026, net income ¥574.4bn. Guidance for H1 FY2027 is ¥1,570bn, a 33% jump, with coater/developer revenue targeted to grow more than 50%, etch more than 25% and advanced packaging more than 60%. TEL is effectively a monopoly in coater/developer systems — the tools that apply and develop photoresist and pair with every ASML scanner — and it sits inside Japan's export control regime, which means India's fab tool set depends on Japanese policy as much as American.

The most instructive foundry in this ledger for India, because it is the strategy India is actually pursuing. Spun out of AMD in 2009 as a Mubadala joint venture, GF walked away from the leading-edge node race and built a top-three pure-play foundry on differentiated specialty platforms instead — RF-SOI, FD-SOI, SiGe, BCD, silicon photonics and embedded memory. FY2025 revenue $6.79bn with net income of $888m and $1.157bn of adjusted free cash flow. It is proof that a viable foundry exists without chasing 2nm, which is the entire thesis behind Dholera.

FY2025 revenue €132.2bn, down 9.2%, with adjusted EBIT of €8.2bn shaped by tariffs, currency and Chinese competition, offset by more than €3.5bn of cost savings. Return on sales at Mercedes-Benz Cars fell to 5.0%. India is a value-over-volume market for it: 19,007 units in 2025 with the average selling price reaching about $111,000, and a record ~$1.5bn of Indian revenue in FY2025. Its Bengaluru R&D centre is its largest outside Germany — India engineers these cars and builds almost none of them.

BMW closed the gap on Mercedes in India in 2025 — 17,271 units against 18,026, up from 14,375 the year before — by competing hard in the entry-luxury segment Mercedes explicitly walked away from. The X1 was its top seller. It runs BMW TechWorks India for software engineering and assembles at Chennai from kits. On motorcycles the comparison inverts: TVS builds BMW's small-capacity bikes, and Royal Enfield outsells BMW Motorrad many times over.

The largest of the three by volume, spanning Volkswagen, Skoda, Audi, Porsche, Lamborghini, Bentley and heavy trucks through Traton. Q4 2025 deliveries fell on softer Chinese and US demand. Its India position is the most substantive of the German three: the MQB-A0-IN platform localised to roughly 95%, Pune and Aurangabad manufacturing, and — the interesting part — a component supply agreement with Mahindra for MEB electric drive units and cells, which is a German group supplying an Indian OEM rather than the reverse.

The premium tyre specialist, sole supplier to Formula 1 and fitted as original equipment to most European performance cars. India is a genuine tyre power — MRF, Apollo, CEAT and JK Tyre hold the domestic market outright, and Balkrishna Industries is a world leader in off-highway tyres exporting from Bhuj. What India does not hold is the ultra-high-performance OE approval that Pirelli lives on.

Trucks, buses, powertrain through FPT Industrial and defence vehicles through Iveco Defence. This is one of the European entries where India is not the weaker party: Tata Motors and Ashok Leyland are among the world's larger commercial vehicle makers, and India builds more buses than almost anyone.

Included because it defines the ceiling of the automotive value chain: roughly 14,000 cars a year at margins no volume manufacturer approaches, sustained by brand, motorsport and deliberate scarcity. India has no entrant at any point of it — and the interesting question the card poses is whether that matters, since the capability is brand and racing heritage rather than manufacturing.

Vespa, Aprilia, Moto Guzzi and the Ape three-wheeler, which Piaggio has built at Baramati in Maharashtra for decades. It is one of the few cards where the Indian firms are unambiguously larger: Hero MotoCorp, Bajaj and TVS are among the biggest two-wheeler makers on earth, and Bajaj is the world's largest three-wheeler manufacturer.

A cooperative from Imola that holds the machinery for ceramic tiles, sanitaryware, closures and beverage filling. It matters enormously and quietly for India: the Morbi cluster in Gujarat makes India the world's second-largest ceramic tile producer, and it runs substantially on Sacmi and System Ceramics presses from Italy.

A family-held Bologna firm holding in-process gauging — measuring a part while the machine is still cutting it, which is what makes precision manufacturing repeatable rather than merely possible. It is the Italian equivalent of a Mittelstand chokepoint and sits under every precision gap in this ledger.

A family-held Bologna firm making gearboxes, gearmotors and drives for industrial, mobile and wind applications, with substantial Indian manufacturing at Chennai and Pune. India competes here more than in most European categories — Elecon and Shanthi Gears are real — but loses at the precision and wind gearbox end.

Segment: Engineering & technology licensing for process plants
ExportControlNote: Tecnimont's parent, and one of the largest engineering contractors working in India — it has built fertiliser, petrochemical and refinery plants across the country for decades. The distinction that matters is between executing a plant and owning the process it runs: Maire's NextChem arm licenses technology, and Indian EPC firms mostly execute foreign licences.

Prime contractor for Europe's Vega launcher and the maker of the solid boosters on Ariane 6 — and one of the very few incumbents in this ledger where India is arguably ahead. ISRO's launch cadence and cost per kilogram beat Vega's, and Skyroot and Agnikul are further along than most European launch startups.

De'Longhi, Kenwood, Braun household and Nutribullet — the premium end of small domestic appliances. India makes small appliances at enormous volume through Havells, Bajaj Electricals, Butterfly and Stovekraft, and does not hold the premium categories where brand and mechanism engineering carry the margin.

The largest machine tool builder in the world by revenue, formed from Gildemeister and Mori Seiki, and the firm that defines five-axis simultaneous machining. It belongs in this ledger for a specific reason: when Kaushik Mudda and Navin Jain showed India's first indigenous five-axis CNC machine, Indian buyers told them only Germans and Japanese could build one. Ethereal Machines built it anyway — roughly 3,200 parts per machine, with precision requirements the Indian supply chain could not meet.

Taiwan's consumer and small-business networking brand, and the eleventh Taiwanese firm in this ledger. It matters less for its size than for the layer it occupies: the ledger has enterprise and data centre networking well covered through Tejas, and almost nothing on the routers, access points and cameras that actually sit in Indian homes and small offices. That tier is held by D-Link, TP-Link and Netgear, and D-Link India Ltd is a listed Indian company under Taiwanese control.

Not to be confused with Motorola Mobility, the smartphone business Lenovo owns and which this ledger already logs as a Tier B trap. Motorola Solutions is what remained after the 2011 split: land mobile radio, command centre software and video security for police, fire, ambulance and defence. India divides sharply on it — Bharat Electronics builds software-defined radios for the armed forces on genuine Indian design authority, while state police and emergency services run largely on imported TETRA and P25 systems.

Founded 2020 in London by Carl Pei, backed by Tiger Global, GV and Highland Europe at a $1.3bn valuation after a $200m Series C. It belongs in this ledger because of a claim rather than a scale: Pei has said he intends to build “India's first truly global smartphone brand” through CMF, which Nothing is spinning off as an independent entity headquartered in India for R&D, manufacturing and export. India is already its largest market at roughly 2% share and its fastest-growing, up 85% year on year in Q2 2025 after 577% in 2024. The $100m joint venture with Optiemus Infracom adds 1,800 jobs on top of $200m already invested. CMF was legally incorporated in India on 7 January 2026 and now has its own entry in this ledger. Whether that produces an Indian brand or an Indian factory for a British one turns entirely on an equity structure neither party has published.

On 7 January 2026 CMF was incorporated as a separate legal entity in India, announced by Nothing co-founder Akis Evangelidis with the certificate itself — “built from India, to the world.” It is the sharpest live test of this ledger's central distinction. Headquarters, R&D, manufacturing and export base are Indian. The brand was created in London in 2023, the parent is Nothing, ties to the parent group are retained, and the ownership structure of the Optiemus joint venture has not been disclosed. On the ledger's own definition that makes it Tier B until equity says otherwise — and it is the most interesting Tier B entry here, because most arrive by acquisition and this one is being built in India on purpose.

The largest omission in this ledger until now, because Arm is not a chip company — it is the architecture underneath almost every chip India assembles. FY2026 revenue $4.92bn, up 23%, a third consecutive year above 20% growth: royalties $2.61bn on virtually every smartphone shipped worldwide, licensing $2.31bn, with data centre royalties more than doubling and its share of hyperscaler CPU compute reaching 50%. Roughly 90% held by SoftBank, with the top five customers about 56% of revenue. Arm's own 20-F names the threat plainly: many of its customers back RISC-V, and if that support grows they may use the free, open architecture instead. India has bet on exactly that.

Two things sit under the Nokia name in India and they point opposite ways. Nokia Networks runs one of its largest plants at Sriperumbudur near Chennai, exporting radio equipment, alongside major R&D in Bengaluru — and Tejas Networks displaced it and Ericsson on BSNL's 4G tender, one of the clearest Indian wins in this ledger. Nokia Technologies is the other half: a standard-essential patent portfolio that collects a royalty on devices, including those assembled in India. The brand on phones is licensed to HMD, not Nokia's own business. And the memory of the Sriperumbudur handset plant, once among the world's largest and closed in 2014 after a tax dispute that cost tens of thousands of jobs, still shapes how India negotiates with telecom vendors.

The purest radio access network business of the western vendors, manufacturing at Pune and running large Indian R&D. Its India story is defined by two things: losing BSNL's 4G core network tender to a Tata-owned Tejas Networks stack — an Indian carrier choosing Indian equipment at national scale — and the standard-essential patent litigation it pursued against Micromax, Intex and Lava, which Indian OEMs largely lost. That litigation is the concrete instance of the SEP chokepoint this ledger logs in the abstract: India can build the network and still pay for the standard it runs on.

Founded 2016 to license the Nokia brand, backed by Google, Qualcomm and Nokia Technologies. It is the third instance in this ledger of the same pattern — alongside Nothing and CMF — of a foreign firm making India its manufacturing and export base while the brand sits abroad, and the most advanced version of it: essentially all HMD phones sold in India are made in India, through Dixon Technologies and Lava, with Zetwerk's Zet Town added for feature phone capacity. It is also the closing of a circle. India lost Nokia's Sriperumbudur plant in 2014; the Nokia brand came back through a licensee, and that licence runs to the end of 2026, which is why HMD has been launching phones under its own name.

The world's largest US-headquartered OSAT and the second largest globally behind ASE, with $6.71bn of 2025 revenue and record advanced packaging and computing revenue. It matters to India because packaging is the one semiconductor layer India has actually entered — Micron at Sanand, Kaynes Semicon at Sanand, CG Power with Renesas and Stars at Sanand, Tata at Jagiroad. Amkor is what those plants are trying to become, and the distance is measured in advanced packaging rather than conventional assembly.

The second-tier pure-play foundry that chose specialty and mature nodes over the leading-edge race, and one of the firms India's fab programme is implicitly benchmarked against. Display driver, power management and RF foundry services all sit here — the process classes Indian fabless startups in power, RF and edge AI actually need, and which Dholera does not offer.

The single most consequential foreign technology partner in India's semiconductor programme. Powerchip licenses the process technology behind Tata Electronics' Dholera fab — India's first commercial fab, targeting 28nm and above. That is the reason Dholera is logged Tier C rather than Tier A throughout this ledger: India will own the plant, the capital and the operation, and the process technology inside it is Powerchip's. Not to be confused with Powertech Technology (PTI), a separate Taiwanese firm in memory packaging that also has its own entry here.

The world's largest memory packaging and test provider, from Hsinchu, and the merchant OSAT behind a large share of DRAM and NAND that ships without an in-house line. It matters to India for a specific reason: Micron's Sanand plant does exactly this work, in-house and foreign-owned, and it is India's flagship semiconductor investment. PTI is what a domestic, Indian-owned version would look like at scale. Not to be confused with PSMC (Powerchip), the Taiwanese foundry licensing process technology to Tata at Dholera — a separate firm with its own entry.

Japan's largest semiconductor company, formed from the Hitachi, Mitsubishi and NEC chip divisions, and a leader in automotive microcontrollers. Its India position runs both directions at once. It bought Steradian Semiconductors of Bengaluru outright in October 2022 — India's 4D imaging radar pioneer, acquired for the team and the patents before it scaled. And it is the technology partner in CG Semi at Sanand, where the equity is the striking part: CG Power holds 92.3%, Renesas 6.8% and Stars Microelectronics 0.9%, on a ₹7,600 crore project ramping to 4.7 billion units a year. Indian-controlled ownership, foreign technology know-how — a better structure than most in this ledger.

The Taiwanese panel maker that moved deliberately away from commodity TV glass toward automotive, industrial, medical and premium displays, buying Germany's BHTC to get automotive cockpit and HMI systems. That shift matters for India specifically: India assembles millions of vehicles a year, every one of them carries displays, and the automotive display is a qualified, long-life, high-margin product India imports entirely.

The partner in the display fab India nearly built. The Vedanta-Innolux joint venture would have been India's first panel plant and was shelved, and nobody has attempted one since. Innolux itself has been converting panel capacity toward fan-out panel-level packaging for semiconductors — a route from displays into advanced packaging that India, holding neither, cannot take.

Segment: Mask blanks, optical glass & medical optics
ExportControlNote: An unusual company and an unusually consequential one: eyeglass lenses and endoscopes in one half, and in the other, the glass blanks that every photomask in the world is made from. Hoya holds EUV mask blanks close to a monopoly and hard disk glass substrates in a similar position — two upstream materials chokepoints that sit beneath lithography and storage respectively, and that almost nobody outside the industry can name. India's answer is at the opposite end of the same company: Aurolab, the manufacturing arm of Aravind Eye Care, makes intraocular lenses at a fraction of Western cost and exports them to well over a hundred countries.

A materials company that turns up underneath four separate chokepoints in this ledger without holding a single consumer-facing product. Battery separator film, dialysis membranes, chlor-alkali ion exchange membranes and semiconductor dry film — each a thin polymer layer that decides whether the system above it works, each held by two or three firms globally. India runs one of the world's largest chlor-alkali industries and one of its largest dialysis populations, and imports the membranes for both.

Founded 1885, and one of the few incumbents in this ledger where India's position is genuinely strong on the headline product and absent on two things underneath it. Optical fibre and cable is an Indian success — Sterlite makes its own preform, and HFCL, Birla Cable and Polycab compete. What India does not make is the fusion splicer that joins every fibre it lays, a category Fujikura and Sumitomo hold between them, or the high-temperature superconducting tape that Fujikura supplies to fusion energy and magnet programmes worldwide.

Founded 1907 as Asahi Glass and renamed AGC in 2018, and the second name behind a striking number of chokepoints already in this ledger — display glass, EUV mask blanks, chlor-alkali membranes and semiconductor fluorochemicals. It is the counterweight to Corning across most of them, which matters because a duopoly is a different risk from a monopoly. India's glass industry is real at container and architectural class and absent at every electronic tier: AGI Greenpac and Hindusthan National Glass make bottles, Saint-Gobain dominates flat glass under French ownership, and nobody makes display substrate, cover glass or mask blanks.

The most chokepoint-dense company in this ledger. Carbon fibre, reverse osmosis membranes, battery separator film, TAC display film and dialysis membranes are five separate materials positions, each held by two to four firms globally, and Toray is in all of them. Carbon fibre is the sharpest: Toray is the world leader, aerospace-grade PAN precursor is export-controlled, and India has been on the wrong side of that control — which is why ISRO, DRDO and NAL developed their own precursor chemistry rather than buying it.

Segment: LNG, car carriers & dry bulk shipping
ExportControlNote: One of Japan's big three shipping lines and among the largest LNG carrier operators in the world. Its India relevance is direct and structural: India is a major LNG importer, and the ships that bring it are Japanese, Greek and Qatari owned. The Shipping Corporation of India has held stakes in LNG carriers serving Petronet through joint ventures with MOL and its peers — minority Indian ownership on vessels carrying Indian cargo, crewed substantially by Indian seafarers, built in Korean yards.

IndianChampion: None at printhead or crystal class
ExportControlNote: Best known for printers, and that is the least consequential thing about it here. Epson makes the piezo printheads that drive industrial inkjet — including the digital decoration lines in Morbi's tile cluster and the textile printers across Surat and Tiruppur — and it is among the world's largest makers of quartz crystal timing devices, which sit inside essentially every electronic product India assembles. Two components almost nobody names, both imported completely, both feeding industries where India is a global volume leader.

IndianChampion: Zeus Numerix (sole Indian CAE product company)
ExportControlNote: CATIA, SOLIDWORKS, SIMULIA and the 3DEXPERIENCE platform — the design and simulation software under most of European aerospace, automotive and industrial engineering. The CAE layer is one of the purest software chokepoints in this ledger: India has roughly a fifth of the world's engineering workforce, runs enormous simulation service businesses through Cyient, LTTS and Tata Elxsi, and has one product company, Zeus Numerix.

A wave of venture-funded CFD startups attacking a market Ansys and Siemens have held for thirty years, most of them built GPU-native or cloud-native rather than porting legacy solvers. Named on the Threadmoat market map: Navier, DotBlocks, Voxshell, Godela, Luminary, Vento, ReynKo, Dive and Flexcompute. India has none of them, which is the point of listing them — this is the challenger layer where entry is currently possible.

The platform layer of the challenger wave: JuliaHub, Volcano, SolverX, SimScale, Fainite, eigenspacedesign, BQP, QuanScient and Rescale. Several are attacking coupled multiphysics, which is where Ansys is strongest, and two — BQP and QuanScient — are betting on quantum-inspired and quantum methods. India has world-class HPC operations through C-DAC and none of this software layer.

Secondmind, ToffeeX, oorja, Coreform, Intact Solutions and Sileom — the structural analysis challengers, several working on meshless and spline-based methods that sidestep the meshing bottleneck rather than automating it. Structural FEA underpins every certification programme in aerospace, civil and automotive engineering, and India certifies on foreign solvers.

PhysicsX, CognaSIM, KronosAI, Key Ward, BeyondMath and Pasteur Labs — firms replacing or accelerating physics solvers with learned surrogates, which is the most genuinely new category on this map and the one where thirty years of incumbent solver validation counts for least. It is also the category where India's AI talent depth should translate most directly, and has not.

Synera, VSIM, Duality, Collimator, Sedaro and Divergent Physics — system-level modelling, control simulation and digital twins, including Sedaro on spacecraft. India builds satellites, launchers, vehicles and factories, and models them in foreign software while its IT services firms are among the world's largest digital twin implementers.

MaterialsZone, Terra AI, Material AI, Polymerize and Lattice Robot — materials informatics and lattice or metamaterial design. This is the software layer above the materials chokepoints this ledger records in abundance: carbon fibre, separators, membranes, magnets, alloys. India imports the materials and also the software used to discover them.

Vinci, Diabatix, heatshape and Nitrexo on thermal and heat transfer; Arena, Nullspace and Cenos on electromagnetics, RF and signal integrity. The EM side matters most for India: Simyog, an IISc spin-off, is one of the very few Indian simulation product companies, working on electromagnetic compatibility for electronics design — in a country assembling hundreds of millions of devices that must pass EMC certification.
